stops.name: Fremont Street
stops.teaser: The street that lit up with neon and then shut out the cars.
stops.map: Fremont Street, Downtown Las Vegas, NV
stops.clue: Go to Fremont Street in downtown Las Vegas. Look for the huge lit-up canopy overhead and walls of bright signs on both sides.
stops.safety: The area is crowded, loud and open late. Stay on the walking area, stick with your group, and do not enter casinos, which are for adults 21 and over.

story: Fremont Street dates back to 1905, the year Las Vegas itself was founded. It was named for explorer and politician John C. Frémont. It was the first paved street in Las Vegas, in 1925, and it got the city's first traffic light in 1931.

In 1931 the Northern Club received one of the first six gambling licenses issued in Nevada, and the first for Fremont Street. The street became known as 'Glitter Gulch' for its many neon signs, like the cowboy Vegas Vic.
Fremont Street once carried several national highways, including U.S. 93, 95 and 466. In September 1994, it was closed to vehicles to begin construction of the Fremont Street Experience.
stops.fact: Fremont Street got the city's first traffic light in 1931.
stops.disputed: Many people call the Las Vegas Strip the original main street. Wikipedia says Fremont Street, the 'Old Vegas Strip', was the heart of the city's casinos first.

claims.t: Fremont Street was the first paved street in Las Vegas.
Fremont Street has always been closed to cars.
claims.why: Wikipedia says it was closed to vehicles in September 1994.

stops.teaser: A Spanish-style hotel that opened out in what was then the sticks.
stops.map: El Cortez, 600 E Fremont Street, Las Vegas, NV
stops.clue: Go to the corner of Sixth Street and Fremont Street, a block east of the walking area. Look for the cream and orange building with arched walkways and a tall EL CORTEZ sign.
stops.safety: Fremont Street has busy traffic. Use crosswalks and view the building from the sidewalk. Casino areas are 21 and over.

story: El Cortez opened on Fremont Street on November 7, 1941. It is one of the oldest casino-hotel properties in Las Vegas and was downtown's first major resort. It is mostly Spanish Colonial Revival in style, though a 1952 remodel modernized the front.

The location at 6th Street and Fremont was originally considered too far from downtown, but the hotel quickly became very profitable. The first hotel had 59 rooms. A tower addition opened in 1984, and the hotel now has 364 rooms.

El Cortez was added to the National Register of Historic Places on February 22, 2013. Wikipedia says it is one of the few Las Vegas casinos that has never changed its exterior facade, keeping the same signage and ranch-themed look for over seventy years.
stops.fact: The original hotel had just 59 rooms.
stops.disputed: Many people assume Las Vegas hotels are always rebuilt. Wikipedia says El Cortez has kept its signage and ranch-themed look for over seventy years, though the front was remodeled in 1952.

claims.t: El Cortez was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1941.

stops.clue: Go to 401 South Fourth Street, just off Las Vegas Boulevard. Look for the white Spanish-style building with a red tile roof and rounded arches.
stops.safety: Use crosswalks around the busy downtown streets. It is a working building with offices and classes, so view it from the sidewalk and enter only when it is open.

story: The Las Vegas Grammar School, also called the Historic Fifth Street School, was built in 1936. It replaced Clark County High School, which operated from 1917 to 1934 and was destroyed by fire. The school sits on a 20-acre site at 401 South Fourth Street.

People came to call it the Fifth Street School because Las Vegas Boulevard was still called Fifth Street. The school was used until 1966. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places on May 20, 1988.

The building has been through a $9.5 million renovation. Today it is home to the city's Office of Cultural Affairs, the Nevada School of Arts and the UNLV School of Architecture's Downtown Design Center.
stops.fact: The school replaced a high school that burned down.
stops.disputed: Many people assume this was always called Fifth Street School. Wikipedia says that was an informal nickname for the Las Vegas Grammar School.

claims.why: Wikipedia says it was used until 1966.

stops.name: Hoover Dam
stops.teaser: A huge concrete dam about 30 miles from the city.
stops.map: Hoover Dam, Black Canyon, NV/AZ border
stops.clue: This is an optional day trip about 30 miles southeast of Las Vegas. At the dam, look for the four round intake towers standing beside the curved concrete wall.
stops.safety: The road to the dam has traffic, heat and a security checkpoint. Go with an adult, bring water, stay behind the railings and on marked walkways, and follow staff directions.

story: Hoover Dam is a concrete arch-gravity dam in the Black Canyon of the Colorado River, on the border between Nevada and Arizona. It was built between 1931 and 1936 during the Great Depression, and dedicated on September 30, 1935 by President Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Thousands of workers built it, and more than 96 lost their lives. The consortium Six Companies, Inc. began construction in early 1931, and the dam was turned over to the federal government on March 1, 1936, more than two years ahead of schedule.
The dam impounds Lake Mead. It is near Boulder City, Nevada, about 30 miles (48 km) southeast of Las Vegas, and about 7 million tourists visit each year.
stops.fact: The dam was finished more than two years ahead of schedule.
stops.disputed: Many people think it has always been called Hoover Dam. Wikipedia says the Roosevelt administration named it Boulder Dam, and Congress restored the name Hoover Dam in 1947.

claims.t: Hoover Dam was turned over to the federal government on March 1, 1936.
Hoover Dam was built in only one year.
claims.why: Wikipedia says construction ran from 1931 to 1936.
